Variants elsewhere usually use bamboo, and modern ones are also made from a paper-towel tube, nails or toothpicks. Factory-made versions are mostly clear plastic tube, filled with small plastic beads and also with seeds, steel balls or sand. The materials of the other parts are not stated.

The rain drum, also called the rain stick, is a long hollow tubular idiophone, with the Hornbostel–Sachs number 112.13+133.1. The body is traditionally made of bamboo or dried cactus, with small pins or spines set in a spiral inside and filled with hard grains such as small stones, seeds, beans or sand. To play, the body is turned and then stood upright, and the grains fall along the inner projections with a rustling sound like rain. Its origin is connected with Chile and Peru in South America, where traditional communities used it to pray to the sky for rain; it also appears in folk music, occasionally enters formal music, and has separate developments in Africa and Asia.
雨鼓音色輕柔飄渺，帶有神秘的詩意質感。其音域屬中高音域，音響飄飄然如絲雨灑落，具: The rain drum's timbre is soft and ethereal, with a mysterious, poetic quality. Its range is in the upper middle register, and its sound drifts like fine rain, warm yet still clear. Because it sounds as an idiophone, it resonates through the body itself, so the sound decays naturally and the timbre is gentler and more contained than traditional drums. Unlike the explosive force of a drum kit, the rain drum is closer to the calm elegance of wind chimes or a xylophone; compared with the deep weight of the timpani it is lighter and more mobile. As a whole it creates a quiet, meditative atmosphere, well suited to poetic and gentle musical settings, and it is highly expressive and artistic.
雨鼓（Rainstick）屬體鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 1: The rain stick is an idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 112.13+133.1. A beginner should first check that both ends of the body are properly sealed and that it contains small stones, rice, dried beans or other hard grains. To play, turn the long hollow tube slowly from horizontal to upright so that the grains slide along the spiral of pins, spines or dividers inside; the slower the turn and the closer to vertical the angle, the longer the grains take to fall and rub, and the easier it is to produce a continuous rustling like rain. Traditional and modern materials include bamboo, dried cactus and clear plastic tube, and the order of operations is the same.
雨鼓（雨聲器）在薩克斯分類法中屬體鳴樂器，編號 112.13+133.1。其起源: The rain stick is an idiophone in the Sachs classification, number 112.13+133.1. Its origin is connected with the rain-making rituals of communities in the Chile and Peru region of South America: the Mapuche made a tube from dried cactus, drove the spines back into the inside and put in small stones, and turning it produced a sound like rain; it is also found further north along the coast of Chile and may likewise be connected with Inca practice. Bamboo variants later developed independently in Southeast Asia, Central Asia, Australia and Africa. Today it is mass-produced from clear plastic tube, paper rolls, nails or toothpicks, and it has become a common instrument in folk music, street performance and healing settings, as well as a frequent tourist item in Latin America and the southwestern United States.
